chohealth.name: CHOHEALTH
chohealth.tagline: Healthcare booking, self-hosted end to end
chohealth.description: An end-to-end telemedicine platform: appointment scheduling, online payments, medical consultations, prescriptions, lab orders, invoicing and pharmacy delivery — built and deployed entirely on my own infrastructure.
chohealth.problem: Small clinics were juggling paper schedules and disconnected tools for booking, billing and records — nothing talked to each other, and double-bookings were routine.
chohealth.stats: 25+ database models · 70+ REST endpoints · 40+ frontend routes
features: A scheduling engine that validates working hours, breaks, service duration and appointment conflicts before a slot is confirmed
Three-layer booking protection: frontend validation, DRF serializer validation, and database constraints
Stripe and PayPal payments with idempotent webhook handling and audited refund workflows
Atomic consultation flow — diagnosis, prescriptions and lab orders are created together or not at all
Invoices, prescriptions and lab orders generated as real PDF documents with ReportLab
QR pickup codes, SendGrid transactional email, and full English/Spanish support

docs.problemLong: Booking a doctor, getting a prescription filled, and paying for care are usually three disconnected experiences for a patient — a phone call to schedule, a paper slip for the pharmacy, a separate portal (or none at all) to see the bill. CHOHEALTH is built to unify that flow into a single product: a patient books an appointment, the doctor produces a medical record and prescription during the visit, the patient fills it through an integrated pharmacy with delivery tracking, and every one of those steps generates a consistent, auditable invoice — all in one authenticated session, in the patient's own language. The engineering goal behind the project was not to build another CRUD demo, but to practice the parts of healthcare software that are unforgiving of shortcuts: preventing a double-booked doctor, keeping a financial ledger that cannot silently drift from reality, reconciling two different payment gateways against the same billing model, and enforcing who is allowed to see or do what. This is an active portfolio project, not a finished product.

decisions.title: Django + DRF for the API
decisions.rationale: Mature ORM with real database-level constraints (not just serializer validation), and a batteries-included admin (Jazzmin) that covers internal/staff tooling without building a separate admin app.

decisions.title: Polymorphic Invoice via two nullable one-to-one fields + a CheckConstraint, instead of a generic foreign key
decisions.rationale: Keeps referential integrity and normal SQL joins on Invoice.appointment / Invoice.medicine_order, while a database-level XOR check makes it structurally impossible to bill both — or neither — target from the same invoice, even if a future view has a bug.

decisions.title: Booking conflict prevention enforced at the database layer, not only in view logic
decisions.rationale: A conditional unique constraint on (doctor, date) is the last line of defense against a race condition where two patients pay for the same slot within milliseconds of each other. Application-level checks run first for a fast, friendly error; the constraint is what actually guarantees correctness under concurrency.

decisions.title: Hosted checkout (Stripe Checkout, PayPal redirect) as the primary payment path; Stripe Elements only for saved cards
decisions.rationale: Hosted checkout keeps PCI-DSS scope on the gateway's side instead of the app's. Elements is used narrowly, for the one flow (saving a card for later) where a hosted redirect would be worse UX.

decisions.title: One shared Stripe webhook for both appointments and pharmacy orders, routed by metadata
decisions.rationale: Avoids duplicating webhook signature verification and event handling for two billable entity types; the invoice/payment model already treats them polymorphically, so the webhook mirrors that.

decisions.title: Role stored on the user (user_type) but never trusted alone for authorization
decisions.rationale: Custom DRF permissions (IsDoctor, IsPatient) check the role and that the related profile object actually exists. A user who claims a role without a matching profile is not authorized — closing a gap that a naive request.user.user_type == 'Doctor' check would leave open.

decisions.title: Denormalized doctor rating, kept in sync via signals
decisions.rationale: The doctor list/search is a hot read path; recomputing an average on every request does not scale as reviews grow. A post_save/post_delete signal on Review recalculates and persists the aggregate instead.

decisions.title: DATABASE_URL-driven database selection (PostgreSQL in production via dj-database-url, SQLite fallback locally)
decisions.rationale: Zero-configuration local development with no external dependency, production-grade database in deployment without touching code.

decisions.title: Cloudinary as the media backend
decisions.rationale: Offloads file storage, transformation and CDN delivery instead of managing a media server; behaves identically in local development and production.

decisions.title: Native fetch wrapper (src/lib/api.ts) instead of a heavier HTTP client on the frontend
decisions.rationale: One place to attach the JWT bearer token, the Accept-Language header, and multipart handling — no extra runtime dependency for what is a thin, predictable API layer.

decisions.title: Next.js App Router with two role-scoped route trees (/dashboard/doctor, /dashboard/patient)
decisions.rationale: File-system routing maps directly onto the two very different user journeys, and each dashboard tree ships only the components its role needs.

docs.businessRulesIntro: The rules below are enforced in code (model constraints, clean() validators, or permission classes), not just described in documentation — each one maps to a specific safeguard in the codebase.

rules: An appointment's clinical status (Unpaid, Confirmed, In Progress, Completed, Cancelled, No Show) is tracked independently from its payment status, which lives on the linked Invoice.

A doctor cannot hold two appointments in a blocking status (Confirmed, In Progress, Completed, No Show) at the same date and time — enforced by a conditional unique constraint at the database level, so Unpaid and Cancelled slots are free to coexist or be retried.
Virtual appointments cannot have a branch assigned; in-person appointments must have one.
Cancellations record who cancelled (patient, doctor, admin, or system) and why; reschedules preserve the original datetime and increment a counter.

A patient cancelling a paid appointment gets a refund percentage set by how much notice they gave: 100% more than 48 hours out, 50% between 24 and 48 hours, 0% inside 24 hours. A doctor-initiated cancellation always refunds 100%, regardless of notice — the patient is never penalized for a doctor's decision.

A doctor's weekly availability (DoctorSchedule) has no self-service API — schedule blocks are created and edited exclusively through the Django admin. A doctor can read their own schedule but not change it from their dashboard.
A medical record is created at most once per appointment and is the anchor for any prescription or lab order tied to that visit.
A prescription line can point to a catalog medication or be free text — a doctor is not blocked from prescribing something outside the hospital's own formulary.

A doctor can only move an appointment along a fixed status graph: Confirmed → In Progress, Completed, Cancelled or No Show; In Progress → Completed or Cancelled. Any other transition is rejected. A virtual appointment cannot move to In Progress without a meeting link set first.

Closing a consultation is a single atomic action: it creates the medical record and, in the same request, an optional prescription and/or lab order together. It cannot be run twice on the same appointment, and none of those three records can be edited or deleted afterward through the API — from the API's perspective, a patient's clinical history is append-only.

Medications and lab tests each declare, independently, two flags: requires_prescription and free_when_prescribed. If requires_prescription is False, a patient can buy or book the item directly, with no doctor involved. If it's True, the purchase or booking endpoint requires an unclaimed prescription item for that exact medication or lab test — issued earlier by a doctor through a completed appointment — and returns 403 otherwise. There is no way to acquire a prescription-gated item without that prior visit.

Pricing for a prescription-gated item is $0 only when it is backed by an unclaimed prescription item and the catalog entry has free_when_prescribed = True (the default); otherwise the patient pays the full catalog price, whether or not a prescription exists.

A prescribed medication (or lab test) can be claimed at most once across all non-cancelled orders — enforced with a one-to-one link between the order line and the source prescription item, so the same prescription can't be dispensed twice through parallel pickup/delivery paths.

Shipping is priced differently depending on which of two distinct pharmacy flows the order goes through: the pharmacy cart (buying medications, prescribed or not, one at a time) always ships free — the per-item price already accounts for it, so claiming a $0 prescribed item through the cart with delivery selected costs nothing at all, shipping included. The dedicated "request delivery" flow (bundling every unclaimed prescribed medication from one prescription into a single delivery order) always charges a flat shipping fee on top, regardless of whether the bundled medications price at $0 or full cost — the only path in the system where shipping is charged.

A pharmacy order's pickup code is generated once, only at the moment it becomes Paid (online payment or fully covered by a prescription); it stays unset while payment is pending, so an unpaid order can never be collected at a branch.

A review can only be submitted for an appointment with status Completed, and only by the patient who owns that appointment; that same patient can later edit or delete it, and only one review exists per appointment.

Review visibility is public, not limited to the author: any patient can browse a feed of every review across every doctor, and a specific doctor's individual reviews are readable even by an unauthenticated visitor. The doctor catalog a patient browses before booking already surfaces each doctor's aggregate rating and review count — a patient is expected to shop by reputation before ever being seen by that doctor, not just rate one afterward.
Every invoice bills exactly one of an appointment or a pharmacy order — never both, never neither — enforced with a database check constraint.
Invoice numbers are sequential per calendar day (INV-YYYYMMDD-NNNN).
Line items store a price snapshot at billing time; later price changes to the underlying service or medication never alter historical invoices.
The sum of completed refunds against a payment can never exceed the original payment amount.
Every payment retains the gateway's raw response alongside a normalized status, so reconciliation never requires going back to Stripe or PayPal support.
Authentication is by email, not username; usernames are derived automatically and de-duplicated with a numeric suffix.
A user's role (Patient / Doctor / Superuser) is necessary but not sufficient for authorization — access also requires the matching profile object to exist.
Access tokens expire after 30 minutes; refresh tokens after 7 days, with rotation enabled so a captured refresh token can be used only once before it is invalidated.

docs.architectureNote: Each Django app owns its own models and views but shares one PostgreSQL/SQLite database; there is no service boundary between them at the data layer, by design — this is a modular monolith, not a microservice system, which matches the project's actual scale and avoids paying a distributed-systems tax it does not need.
docs.schemaIntro: The schema is split across four diagrams that mirror the Django apps, to keep each one legible. Primary keys are UUID-like short IDs (sid) exposed to the API; numeric IDs stay internal.
docs.schemaNote: Invoice.appointment and Invoice.medicine_order are both nullable one-to-one fields; a database CheckConstraint requires exactly one of them to be set, which an entity-relationship diagram cannot express directly — it is enforced in billing/models.py, not only in application code.

notifications.intro: Every transactional email is fire-and-forget — a failed send is logged, never blocks the request — and shares one branded template. Eight distinct triggers exist end to end:

items.when: Doctor marks a virtual appointment In Progress
The patient's own tracking poll detects the final stage

notifications.note: There is currently no welcome email on signup and no "lab results ready" email — both are natural additions, not yet built.

limitations: Delivery tracking is simulated, not real. There is no courier integration, webhook, or geolocation anywhere in the codebase. MedicineDelivery.stage is computed on every poll from elapsed time since the order was paid — 5 fixed stages, 30 seconds each, about 2 minutes end to end — not from any real-world event. The "delivery completed" email is only sent the next time the patient's own client polls the tracking endpoint after the final stage is reached; there is no background worker guaranteeing it fires if the patient never reopens that screen. The next real step here would be a courier webhook (or at minimum a scheduled task instead of client-triggered polling) — genuinely building that out, rather than the current simulation, is on the roadmap.

Doctor availability has no self-service API yet. A doctor's weekly schedule (DoctorSchedule) can currently only be created or edited through the Django admin — there is no "manage my availability" endpoint on the doctor's own dashboard.
roadmap: Secure patient-doctor chat via Medplum — an open-source, FHIR-native healthcare platform. Medplum is being adopted deliberately, not as a generic chat feature: it is built around the encryption, access-control and interoperability standards that healthcare data exchange is generally expected to meet, which is the same bar this integration is meant to hold the project to, rather than building bespoke messaging infrastructure that would need to reinvent those guarantees.
Additional Medplum-backed capabilities (structured FHIR resource sync, clinical data exchange) as the integration matures.

A real delivery-tracking implementation, replacing the current time-based simulation — likely a courier webhook (or, at minimum, a scheduled background task) driving MedicineDelivery.stage off real events instead of elapsed time on read.
A doctor-facing schedule management endpoint, so weekly availability no longer requires the Django admin.

choplanner.name: CHO Planner
choplanner.description: A personal task and note manager in the spirit of Linear or ClickUp, deliberately simpler — with a swappable AI assistant that breaks goals into weighted subtasks and an optional Google Calendar sync.
choplanner.problem: Most task managers either lock you into their cloud or hand your data — and your AI provider's API key — to a third party. I wanted something I fully own: self-hosted, with AI as an optional layer, not a dependency.
features: Swappable AI assistant — bring your own Claude, GPT or Gemini key; every provider's output is validated against the same Zod schema before it touches the database
Kanban board with drag-and-drop, weighted task priorities, sprints and Markdown notes
Optional Google Calendar sync via OAuth 2.0, always with explicit confirmation before writing an event
API keys and refresh tokens encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM — never sent back to the frontend
Installable PWA with an offline page and a service worker that never caches API routes

docs.problemLong: CHO Planner is a task and note manager in the spirit of Linear or ClickUp, but deliberately simpler, built around a customizable AI assistant — with its own avatar, name and personality — that breaks goals down into weighted subtasks and, optionally, syncs work with Google Calendar. The design rests on four principles: local-first (the app works 100% without external services; integrations are additive, never required), Bring Your Own Keys (each user supplies their own credentials — Google account, LLM API key — stored encrypted, so the operator is never a custodian of third-party credentials), mobile-first responsive (one web codebase adapting to phone, tablet and desktop, no native port), and swappable AI (the user picks the provider — Claude, GPT, Gemini — and switching models changes the wording, never the structure of what gets generated).

decisions.title: AI output is never trusted directly — it fills a Zod schema the code defines, validated with retries
decisions.rationale: The model never decides the format or executes actions directly: it only fills a structure defined in code. The code validates the output against that schema before using it and, if it doesn't comply, retries by re-injecting the validation error (max 3 attempts) — this guarantees a roadmap generated by Gemini has exactly the same fields as one from Claude.

decisions.title: A MODEL_REGISTRY declares each model's structured-output support level (full / partial)
decisions.rationale: Not every LLM is equally reliable at returning structured data. Declaring that support level in one place means the UI only offers models for generation that are actually known to comply, instead of letting a user pick a model that will silently produce malformed plans.

decisions.title: API keys and refresh tokens are encrypted with AES-256-GCM and never reach the frontend
decisions.rationale: The BYOK philosophy only holds if credentials are actually protected — chat and generation run entirely on the server, so a compromised frontend can't leak a key it never had.

decisions.title: Google Calendar pushes always require explicit confirmation before writing an event
decisions.rationale: Automating a write to a user's real calendar without confirmation is the kind of integration that erodes trust the first time it does something unexpected — the assistant proposes, the user decides.

decisions.title: Assistant appearance is stored as JSON (avatarConfig), not as rigid columns
decisions.rationale: Avatar parameters vary by avatar library (DiceBear styles each have different configurable traits); a rigid table would force a schema migration every time an avatar style changes.

decisions.title: Task separates title (what) from description (how); Subtask is kept deliberately lightweight
decisions.rationale: A task needs both a goal and a plan for reaching it. A subtask is meant to be an atomic checklist item — if a subtask needs a long description, that's a sign it should be promoted to its own task instead.

decisions.title: CalendarEvent is its own table, reusable across Task, Sprint and Note
decisions.rationale: All three entity types can sync to Google Calendar and need to track a googleEventId to update or delete the same event later — modeling this once as a shared table avoids duplicating that sync logic three times.

docs.architectureNote: Everything lives inside Next.js — Server Actions and Route Handlers — there is no separate backend server. The instance is self-contained: anyone can clone the repository, configure .env, spin up Postgres with Docker, and get a fully working task manager with zero external services. Google Calendar and the LLM provider are optional add-ons, wired in only once the user supplies their own credentials.
docs.schemaIntro: The model revolves around User, the owner of everything in cascade. Ten entities cover identity, content and integrations.

An LLM provider API key, encrypted (AES-256-GCM). Unique per (userId, provider).
OAuth link: encrypted refresh token, scope, calendarId, and syncToken.
Work container with name, description, color, and icon.
Time-boxed grouping of tasks with a goal and dates.
title (what) + description (how), weight 1–10, status, aiGenerated, and position.
Lightweight atomic unit: title + short note + weight + done.
Markdown note, tied to a workspace or standalone, with an optional reminder.
Event reusable by Task, Sprint, or Note; stores the googleEventId to update/delete in Google.

roadmap: Workspaces and tasks with a Kanban board
Drag and drop with order persistence
Multi-provider AI assistant with validated output
PWA: installable, with a service worker and offline page

neurostock.name: Neurostock
neurostock.tagline: Stock price prediction with LSTM neural networks
neurostock.description: Predicts stock prices for any ticker using an LSTM neural network trained on historical data from Yahoo Finance, with backtesting and confidence intervals — not just a single-number guess.
features: 2-layer LSTM (128 + 64 units) trained on up to 10 years of historical price data per ticker
Monte Carlo Dropout (50 iterations) to turn a single prediction into a real confidence interval
Strict separation between train and test scalers to prevent data leakage — a mistake most tutorials skip
Backtesting dashboard with MSE, RMSE and R² computed against real historical prices
JWT auth with automatic token refresh, and a singleton-cached model for fast concurrent predictions

docs.problemLong: NeuroStock is a full-stack web app that predicts stock market prices with a Machine Learning model: an LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) neural network trained on historical data pulled from Yahoo Finance. Every prediction runs through two stages — backtesting, where the model is evaluated against real historical data it never trained on, and a future forecast with confidence intervals, not a single naked number. The project deliberately practices the parts of ML engineering that are easy to fake and easy to get wrong: preventing data leakage between training and test data, quantifying how uncertain a forecast actually is instead of presenting it as fact, and keeping a trained model fast to serve under concurrent requests. This is an educational project — predictions do not constitute financial advice, and stock trading carries real risk of capital loss.

decisions.title: Strict train/test scaler separation to prevent data leakage
decisions.rationale: The MinMaxScaler is fit only on the training split; test data is transformed with that same training-fitted scaler, never refit on its own. Letting the scaler see test-set statistics during training is a subtle mistake most tutorials skip, and it silently inflates backtest accuracy.

decisions.title: Monte Carlo Dropout instead of a single point prediction
decisions.rationale: Running 50 stochastic forward passes with dropout active turns one forecast into a real confidence interval, with a growing uncertainty factor (+2% per day) that reflects how compounding error actually behaves over a longer horizon — instead of presenting a 200-day forecast with the same false confidence as a 1-day one.

decisions.title: Every prediction runs a backtest before it runs a forecast
decisions.rationale: Before showing a future prediction, the model is evaluated against real historical data it was not trained on (70/30 split), and MSE, RMSE and R² are computed and shown alongside the forecast — accountability instead of a black-box number.

decisions.title: Recursive multi-day forecasting from a fixed 100-day-lookback architecture
decisions.rationale: The model only knows how to predict one step ahead from a 100-day window; predicting up to 365 days out means feeding each prediction back in as if it were real data for the next step. This is what makes long-horizon forecasts possible from a single fixed architecture, and it's exactly why uncertainty has to grow with each step instead of staying constant.

decisions.title: The trained LSTM model is cached as a thread-safe singleton
decisions.rationale: Deserializing a Keras model from disk on every request would make concurrent predictions slow and wasteful; ml_manager.py loads it once and holds it in memory, safe for concurrent access.

decisions.title: JWT authentication with refresh token rotation
decisions.rationale: A 15-minute access token limits the exposure window of a leaked token, while a 7-day rotating refresh token keeps the user logged in without asking them to re-authenticate constantly — rotation means a captured refresh token can't be replayed indefinitely.

docs.architectureNote: A client-server split with a clear boundary: the React SPA never touches Yahoo Finance or the model directly, everything goes through the Django REST API. The business-logic layer (DataPipeline, MLManager, PredictionEngine) sits between the API and the ML layer so the view functions stay thin.

steps: A successful login makes the backend generate an access + refresh token pair.
The frontend stores both tokens in localStorage.
The access token expires after 15 minutes.
The frontend uses the refresh token to get a new access token.
If the refresh token has also expired, the frontend logs the user out automatically.

docs.dataModelNote: Stock data itself is not stored anywhere — it's fetched in real time from Yahoo Finance on every prediction. The database only persists user accounts.

model.dataLeakageIntro: The system implements strict separation between training and testing data:
model.uncertaintyNote: Monte Carlo Dropout is used to estimate prediction uncertainty: 50 Monte Carlo iterations per prediction, a growing uncertainty factor (+2% per day), and configurable confidence intervals (80%, 95%, 99%).

rows.description: Run a prediction (backtest + future forecast) for a ticker

limitations: One static, pre-trained model is shared by every ticker — stock_prediction_model.keras is not retrained per stock, so accuracy varies with how closely a given ticker's price behavior resembles what the model was trained on.

Longer forecasts are recursive, not independently modeled — each predicted day is fed back in as input for the next, so error compounds the further out the forecast goes, which is exactly why the confidence interval widens with the horizon instead of staying fixed.

Predictions are educational, not financial advice — the model has no awareness of news, earnings, macroeconomic events or anything outside historical price patterns, and stock trading carries real risk of capital loss.
roadmap: Support for multiple model architectures (GRU, Transformer)

gettingStarted.closingNote: Frontend available at http://localhost:5173. Enter a ticker (e.g. AAPL, TSLA) on the dashboard to see backtesting and a future forecast with confidence intervals.

sevenlever.name: Seven Lever
sevenlever.description: A local two-player dice game based on "Seven Eleven", the game played in Colombian schoolyards — bets, a life bar, and an animated loss sequence, all live in the frontend.
features: The full ruleset: target-number logic, instant loss on 7 or 11, a configurable life bar (3–10 hits)
Game logic runs 100% in the frontend for zero-latency turns — the backend only persists finished rounds
Framer Motion animations for the dice roll, the "seal" hit, and the crying loss sequence
Local two-player state in Zustand; match history and stats persisted through Prisma
Sound effects via Howler.js, lazy-loaded so they never block first paint

docs.problemLong: Seven Lever is a dice game for two players on the same device, based on the classic "Seven Eleven" played in Colombian schoolyards. At the start of each round the stakes are set — cards (an exchange) or seals (a hit with the index and middle finger on the forearm). The active player rolls the dice, and the total from the first valid roll becomes their target number; rolling a 7 or 11 on that very first roll is an instant loss. From there they keep rolling until they either repeat the target number (round won) or hit a 7 or 11 (round lost). In seal mode, the loser's health bar drops, and hitting zero triggers a loss animation — a crying character with a marked-up forearm. The number of seals is configurable between 3 and 10. Since it's a same-device, non-competitive game, the engineering goal was different from a typical CRUD app: keep every turn at zero latency by running the entire game locally, and only talk to the backend to persist what already happened.

decisions.title: No WebSockets — the whole game runs on one device
decisions.rationale: Both players share the same screen and the same session; there's nothing to synchronize in real time between two clients, so a persistent connection would be solving a problem this game doesn't have.

decisions.title: Game logic is 100% frontend and side-effect-free (gameLogic.ts)
decisions.rationale: Dice rolls and round outcomes are evaluated locally for zero-latency turns. Keeping that logic as pure functions, separate from the UI and from any network call, makes it trivial to reason about and test.

decisions.title: The backend only persists finished rounds and games — it never re-validates a roll
decisions.rationale: This is a local, non-competitive game, not an online multiplayer one — there's no cheating to defend against between two people sharing a table. The backend's job is history and stats, not refereeing.

decisions.title: In-progress game state lives in Zustand, in memory — nothing is written until a round or game actually finishes
decisions.rationale: A round that's still being played has no reason to touch the network or the database; persisting only completed outcomes keeps the hot path (rolling dice, seeing the result) instant.

decisions.title: Player is explicitly not an auth concept
decisions.rationale: A Player row is just the display name typed in at game setup — there's no login, no session, no credential to manage, because the game has no notion of an account in the first place.

decisions.title: Sound effects are lazy-loaded with Howler.js
decisions.rationale: Dice-rolling, hit and crying sounds only matter once a game actually starts, so loading them eagerly would just slow down the very first paint for no benefit.

docs.architectureNote: No WebSockets, no real-time sync — it's a local, same-device game. All game logic lives in the frontend; the backend's only job is to persist the outcome once a round or game actually finishes.
docs.schemaIntro: Four models cover the whole game: Player is just a display name (not an auth account), Game is a full match between two players, Round is one target-number cycle within a game, and Roll is a single pair of dice within a round.

rows.description: Create a new game (player names, mode, seal count)
Mark a game finished and record the winner
Global stats (most wins, and so on)

limitations: Same-device only, not online multiplayer. There's no WebSocket layer, no matchmaking, no notion of two clients in different places playing the same match — both players share one screen.

The backend trusts the frontend's dice rolls instead of re-validating them. That's a reasonable trade-off for a local, non-competitive game between two people at the same table, but it means this design would need real server-side validation before it could support any online or competitive mode.

gettingStarted.closingNote: Frontend at http://localhost:3000, API at http://localhost:4000/api. Type in both player names, pick a mode, and start rolling — there's no account to create.

thesis.name: AI-JobMatch
thesis.tagline: AI-powered video interviews, matched to the right vacancy
thesis.category: Bachelor's Thesis — Universidad Tecnológica de Bolívar
thesis.description: A system that transcribes a candidate's video interview, extracts the skills and keywords that matter for a specific vacancy, and scores their affinity against it — built to reduce the time recruiters spend manually screening applicant videos, and the subjective bias that comes with doing it by hand.
thesis.problem: Recruiters reviewing candidates for a position face a large volume of applicant videos they have to watch and evaluate manually. That traditional approach is tedious, time-consuming, and carries a real risk of subjective bias creeping into who gets shortlisted.
thesis.stats: 30 candidates × 10 vacancies tested · 100% correct matches · 3 weighted metrics
features: Transcribes a candidate's video interview with Whisper X and extracts job-relevant keywords with NLP/n-grams
Vectorizes both the transcript and the job description with TF-IDF so they can be compared mathematically
Scores affinity with three combined metrics — cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, and exact skill matching — instead of trusting a single one
Produces a weighted affinity score per candidate–vacancy pair, shown as a 0–100% match or a 0–5 rating
Documented across 6 stakeholder viewpoints — applicants, company, developers, regulators, competitors, technology providers — following IEEE 1471-2000
Validated on a real dataset: 30 candidate transcripts against 10 vacancies, with a 100% correct-match rate

docs.problemLong: AI-JobMatch is the software architecture behind a system that reads a candidate's video interview, transcribes it, and turns that transcript into a quantitative affinity score against a specific job vacancy — the same problem recruiters already solve by hand, at scale. In the traditional process, recruiters review a large volume of candidate videos manually: it's slow, and it leaves room for subjective bias to creep into who gets shortlisted. The system is organized in four layers — presentation (upload and results UI), business logic (orchestrating the pipeline), data access (the datasets and their persistence), and services (shared functionality reused across the pipeline) — and the whole architecture is documented from six separate stakeholder viewpoints (applicants, the hiring company, developers, regulators, competitors, and technology providers), following the IEEE 1471-2000 standard for architecture description, so the design is accountable to more than just the people who built it.

decisions.title: Whisper X (OpenAI) for transcription, chosen specifically for precision
decisions.rationale: Every downstream step — keyword extraction, vectorization, scoring — depends on the transcript being accurate. A high-precision speech-recognition model was a prerequisite, not a nice-to-have, since transcription errors would silently corrupt every metric built on top of them.

decisions.title: Affinity is scored with three combined metrics, not one
decisions.rationale: Cosine similarity and Euclidean distance each give a global, vector-space view of how close a candidate's transcript is to a job description — direction and magnitude, respectively — but neither is sensitive to one specific skill actually being mentioned. A third metric, exact skill matching, adds that precision back in. The three are combined into one weighted score so the result reflects both overall fit and specific requirements.

decisions.title: Keywords are represented with n-grams and TF-IDF vectorization, not raw word matching
decisions.rationale: Comparing isolated keywords loses the context they appear in. Representing transcripts and job descriptions as n-gram vectors, weighted with TF-IDF, captures the structure and relationship between neighboring words — which is what cosine similarity and Euclidean distance actually need to operate on.

decisions.title: A layered architecture — presentation, business logic, data access, services
decisions.rationale: Separating the upload/results UI from the pipeline orchestration, from the datasets, from shared services keeps each concern independently testable and replaceable — swapping the transcription engine, for example, shouldn't require touching how results are displayed.

decisions.title: Six stakeholder viewpoints, documented independently, per IEEE 1471-2000
decisions.rationale: A recruiting tool has stakeholders whose concerns actively conflict — applicants want fairness and privacy, the hiring company wants speed and precision, regulators want auditability. Documenting each viewpoint's concerns and constraints separately, rather than one generic requirements list, makes those tensions explicit instead of papering over them.

decisions.title: Two independent datasets — vacancies and candidate transcripts — related many-to-many
decisions.rationale: A vacancy dataset (title, description, required skills) and a candidate dataset (ID, transcript) are kept separate and can each grow independently — one candidate can apply to many vacancies, and one vacancy can receive many candidates, without the schema forcing a rigid one-to-one pairing.

docs.architectureNote: The system has no notion of real-time collaboration or multi-tenant infrastructure — it's a pipeline: a video comes in, a score comes out. The four layers exist to keep that pipeline's concerns separated, not to support horizontal scale beyond what a single evaluation run needs.
docs.schemaIntro: The data model splits vacancies and candidates into two independent datasets, related many-to-many: one candidate can apply to several vacancies, and one vacancy can receive several candidates.

specs.value: Vector orientation between a candidate's skill profile and a job's requirements — closer to 1 means a stronger match.
Direct geometric distance between the same two vectors — a smaller distance means a stronger match.
Exact overlap between skills explicitly mentioned by the candidate and those required by the vacancy.
The three metrics combined into one affinity score, shown as a 0–100% match or a 0–5 rating.

results: Tested against 30 candidate transcripts and 10 job vacancies, the system found the correct transcript-to-vacancy match in 100% of cases using cosine similarity and Euclidean distance alone.
The third metric, exact skill matching, refined that result further by comparing the specific skills a vacancy requires against the ones a candidate actually mentioned in context.

Cosine similarity and Euclidean distance moved in the expected opposite directions across the test set — higher similarity consistently paired with lower distance — which is the behavior that gives confidence the affinity patterns being detected are real, not noise.
limitations: Results depend heavily on transcription quality — background noise or an inaccurate transcript directly degrades every downstream metric.
The model is more effective on general linguistic contexts and may have limitations processing specific dialects or strong linguistic variation.
If the training data carries bias, the model can reflect that bias in its evaluations — mitigation measures are in place, but complete elimination of bias can't be guaranteed.
Affinity is scored from a single input — the video transcript — by design; it does not account for facial expressions or vocal tone, which could add robustness in a future version.
roadmap: Test the model against a larger synthetic dataset with known expected outcomes, to validate it against a concrete ground truth.
Compare those synthetic-data results against real-world data, to monitor how far actual behavior diverges from the expected baseline at scale.
